callouts.text: It is good that we can open again.

rows.text: Certificates halted after data is found deleted from the Criminal Register
Hundreds of teacher students cannot start placements
Six largest municipalities write to Wammen: the stop is critical

extended.text: The National Police resumed issuing child-protection certificates on Friday afternoon, 16 days after halting them on 2 September over an error in the Criminal Register.

The review found 43 rulings relevant to the certificates had been deleted too early; they have been re-entered. Rulings from before 2011 could not be recreated, but the police judge the register fit for use again and call the error's consequences 'very limited'.
'We are very aware that the pause has caused difficulties for a great many people. So it is good that we can open again,' said Lasse Boje, the national police chief.

On Thursday Copenhagen, Aarhus, Aalborg, Odense, Esbjerg and Randers wrote to justice minister Nicolai Wammen that the stop had created a 'critical and severely disruptive situation'. Around 400 hirings were on hold in Aarhus alone, and the six said they had been told to expect a fix within ten days.
Employers must hold the certificate before anyone works with children. Several hundred teacher students could not begin placements, and KL, the municipalities' association, had asked for a timetable.

short.text: Warren Buffett, 96, is stepping down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman after more than 50 years; his son Howard takes the chair and Buffett stays on the board.

standard.text: Warren Buffett is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway after more than 50 years, the company said on Friday. He is 96, becomes chairman emeritus with immediate effect and stays on the board.
His son Howard Buffett, a director since 1993, takes the chair as part of a long-planned succession.
'Father Time always wins,' Buffett wrote in a letter to shareholders.
Berlingske puts the fortune he built at 940 billion kroner and places him among the ten richest people in the world, behind Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk.

short.text: Copenhagen's city council removed Frie Grønne leader Sikandar Siddique on Thursday after he finally lost a dispute over his residence; the party keeps the seat.

standard.text: Copenhagen's city council removed Sikandar Siddique, leader of Frie Grønne, at its meeting on Thursday evening, after he finally lost a long-running dispute with the municipality over his residence, a case rooted in last year's local election.

The party keeps its seat. Dansk Folkeparti, Venstre and Liberal Alliance abstained when Asham Agha Nadeem was approved as his substitute, calling the seat a deception of voters; the Conservatives criticised the other blue parties for the gesture.
Siddique accepts the decision but says he still does not understand it.

copy.deck: Frie Grønne keeps the seat; three blue parties abstained on his replacement.

callouts.label: tonnes of CO2 to be stored under the North Sea

short.text: The EU's first large-scale CO2 storage opened off Esbjerg on Friday with King Frederik present; Ineos will store 400,000 tonnes under the North Sea, a project a climate group and a think tank criticise for its technology and financing.

standard.text: The first large-scale carbon storage project in the EU opened on Friday, with King Frederik performing the opening. Ineos will pump 400,000 tonnes of CO2 into a depleted oil field under the North Sea, shipped out from Esbjerg.
DR describes the opening as coming after years of disappointments for Danish politicians over carbon storage; the Financial Times notes a separate Norwegian site opened shortly before.

Berlingske reports the company is 'proud' of the project while a climate organisation and a think tank criticise both its technology and its financing. Dansk Fjernvarme, the district-heating trade body, calls the day a milestone for carbon capture in Denmark and the EU.

copy.deck: Ineos will store 400,000 tonnes in an old oil field; a climate group and a think tank call the technology doubtful.
copy.headline: King Frederik opens the EU's first large-scale CO2 store under the North Sea

short.text: Dansk Folkeparti is twice Venstre's size in a new poll and the largest party in the blue bloc; Altinget ties Venstre's fall to its split over the fertiliser law and has measured it lower only once before.

standard.text: Dansk Folkeparti is now twice as large as Venstre in a new poll, the largest party in the blue bloc by a wide margin and the second-largest in the Folketing.
Altinget attributes Venstre's fall to the split in the party after the fertiliser law was passed, and says its monthly poll has measured Venstre lower only once before.
An analyst on DR calls Venstre's position an 'identity crisis'. Kristeligt Dagblad quotes the party's own reading: voters are punishing it for internal unrest.

copy.deck: Only once has Altinget's monthly poll measured Venstre lower.
